channel.title: Visual on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Visual on Best of AI

item.title: Adobe Illustrator
item.description:
Illustrator draws with vectors, meaning shapes are stored as paths and curves instead of pixels, so artwork can be scaled to any size without losing sharpness. That makes it the standard tool for logos, icons, packaging, infographics, and print layouts. Designers build artwork with the Pen tool, shape builders, gradients, and precise typography, and the finished files can go straight to a printer, a website, or a sign shop.

Its AI features aim to speed up the repetitive parts of the job. Text to Vector Graphic generates editable vector shapes from a description. Generative Recolor tries a set of color palettes on an existing design based on a prompt, and Image Trace converts a sketch or photo into vector outlines. Other tools help with selections, pattern creation, and mockups. The output is real vector art on proper layers, so it can be edited like anything else you draw.

item.title: Adobe Photoshop
item.description:
Photoshop is the image editor most photographers, retouchers, and designers learn first. It works on pixels in layers, with masks, selections, adjustment layers, and blend modes that let you change one part of an image without touching the rest. Photo retouching, product shots, poster layouts, and web graphics all fit into that same layer-based workflow, which is why files and techniques carry from one studio to the next.

The AI features sit inside that workflow instead of replacing it. Generative Fill takes a selection and a short text prompt and creates new content that matches the lighting and perspective around it. Generative Expand extends the canvas past the original edges, and the Remove tool erases distractions like power lines or stray people. Select Subject and Neural Filters handle selections, portrait adjustments, and colorization with less manual work. Generated content arrives on its own layer, so you can mask it, blend it, or throw it away.

item.title: Affinity
item.description:
Affinity grew from a set of three separate apps: Photo, Designer, and Publisher. These are now combined in a single application, so a designer can retouch an image, draw vector artwork, and lay out a page without switching programs. It’s non-destructive, supports layers and masks, and opens common files including PSD and AI. It became popular as an alternative to Adobe software for people who disliked subscriptions.

Canva acquired the Affinity company and now offers the unified app for free to individuals, with the option to connect to Canva for sharing and collaboration. Organizations that need features like single sign-on can arrange enterprise or education plans. AI tools are optional and tied to a Canva premium plan, so users who prefer to avoid AI can skip them. Integration lets you send designs to Canva and bring them back.

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: Bria
item.description:
Bria builds visual generative AI around licensing. Its models are trained on licensed data from content partners rather than scraped web images, and contributors share in revenue, which gives companies a clearer position on copyright than many alternatives. The company also offers indemnification to enterprise customers.

The product is delivered as APIs and tools for businesses. Capabilities include generating images from prompts, editing and background removal, creating product shots, and controls for brand consistency. Enterprises in advertising, e-commerce, and media can embed these features in their apps, with options for fine-tuning on their own assets.

item.title: Capture One
item.description:
Capture One began as software for tethered shooting, where a camera connects to a computer and photos appear on screen immediately, and it’s still a leader there. Studio and commercial photographers like its fast, reliable tethering, strong RAW processing, and color tools, including detailed color editing, skin tone adjustment, and support for many camera profiles. It offers a catalog system and sessions for organizing shoots.

Editing features include layers and masks, advanced color grading, and tools for sharpening and noise reduction. AI is used for masking, such as selecting subjects and backgrounds, and for other tasks that speed up workflow. A mobile app and live collaboration features let clients and teams review images during a shoot, and it works across Mac and Windows.

item.title: Claude Design
item.description: Claude Design lets you make visual material by talking to Claude. Instead of dragging shapes in an editor, you ask for what you need, such as a slide deck for a product update, a landing page mockup, or a clickable prototype, and Claude builds a first version. You refine it with follow-up messages, like asking for a calmer color palette, a different layout, or an extra section, and the design updates.

item.title: Coolors
item.description:
Coolors makes picking colors quick and fun. You open the generator, press the spacebar, and it produces a harmonious five-color palette. You can lock the colors you like and keep generating until the rest fit, adjust hue, saturation, and brightness, and see names and codes for each color. It is used by web designers, brand designers, illustrators, and anyone choosing colors for a project.

Several tools extend the generator. You can extract a palette from a photo, check color contrast for accessibility, preview palettes on mockups, explore thousands of palettes shared by the community, and export in many formats including CSS, SVG, and code for design tools. Plugins connect to Figma, Adobe apps, and browsers. AI features can generate palettes from a text description or mood.

item.title: DxO PhotoLab
item.description:
DxO PhotoLab builds on years of lab testing of cameras and lenses. When you open a RAW file, it automatically applies corrections specific to your camera and lens combination for distortion, vignetting, and sharpness, which gives a solid starting point. The editor then provides tools for exposure, color, tone, and detail, with local adjustments using masks and control points inherited from the Nik Collection, which DxO owns.

Its noise reduction is its best-known feature. DeepPRIME XD uses AI to remove noise and recover detail from high-ISO images, and many photographers rate it among the best available, especially for low-light work. Other tools include ClearView for contrast, color rendering profiles, and lens sharpness adjustments. It works as a standalone editor and as a plugin with Lightroom or Photoshop, and DxO also sells PureRAW for batch processing.

item.title: Flourish
item.description:
Flourish makes data storytelling accessible. Users upload a spreadsheet, pick a template such as a bar chart race, scatter plot, hierarchy, map, or scrolling story, and customize colors, labels, and animations. The result is an interactive graphic that can be embedded in a website or article, or exported as an image or video.

Its biggest draw is the library of templates, including formats that are hard to build by hand, like animated race charts and data-driven stories that change as the reader scrolls. Teams can set up brand themes, collaborate on projects, and update charts when data changes. Newsrooms and organizations use it to publish clear graphics quickly.

item.title: GIMP
item.description: GIMP, the GNU Image Manipulation Program, has been a mainstay of free software for decades. It handles photo retouching, compositing, and digital painting with layers, masks, curves, selection tools, brushes, and a large set of filters. It reads and writes many file formats, including PSD files to a degree, and supports scripting in Python and Script-Fu for automation. The latest major version brought improvements such as non-destructive editing and better color management.

item.title: Google Stitch
item.description:
Stitch is designed to get from an idea to an interface quickly. You describe an app screen or a website, upload a sketch or screenshot, and Stitch generates a designed layout with components, colors, and text, which you can modify through further prompts or by editing directly. It can produce multiple variations, so you can explore directions before settling on one.

Output is meant to be practical. Designs can be pasted into Figma for further work by designers, or exported as front-end code, such as HTML and CSS, to give developers a starting point. The tool incorporates technology from Galileo AI, which Google acquired, and runs on Gemini models, with experimental features that improve over time.

item.title: Inkscape
item.description:
Inkscape is a capable vector editor that costs nothing. Users draw with pens, shapes, and text, and the results are stored as scalable vector graphics, which remain sharp at any size. It includes tools for paths, boolean operations, gradients, patterns, and a trace feature that converts bitmaps to vectors. Designers use it for logos, icons, illustrations, laser cutting files, and web graphics.

As an open-source project, it has a community that builds extensions and shares resources. Its SVG-centered design makes it a good fit for web work, and it can export to PNG, PDF, and other formats, and import many common file types. The interface has improved significantly in recent versions, and it runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. AI features are not built into the core, though plugins and external tools add some.

item.title: Invoke
item.description:
Invoke is built for people who want control over AI images. Beyond typing a prompt, the layered canvas lets users paint, mask, and inpaint specific areas, combine generated elements, and iterate on a composition like in an image editor. Control features guide pose, depth, and structure.

It works with Stable Diffusion and other open models, and users can add their own checkpoints and fine-tunes. The open-source release runs on a local machine with a capable GPU, which keeps images private, and the company provides a hosted version for teams with management features.

item.title: Mentimeter
item.description:
Mentimeter makes presentations interactive. You build slides with questions such as multiple choice polls, word clouds, rating scales, rankings, and open-ended questions, share a join code or QR code, and the audience responds from their phones. Results appear live on the screen, which turns a one-way talk into a conversation and gives quiet participants an easy way to contribute.

It suits a range of settings. Teachers use it to check understanding, trainers to energize workshops, and companies to run all-hands meetings and collect anonymous feedback. Features include quizzes with leaderboards, Q&A with upvoting, and templates, and you can import existing slides from PowerPoint or Google Slides. AI helps generate a presentation from a prompt, suggest questions, and summarize responses.

item.title: NocoDB
item.description:
NocoDB turns a database into something that feels like Airtable. Connect it to an existing SQL database or create a new one, and users see tables as spreadsheets they can filter, sort, and edit, with views as kanban boards, galleries, calendars, and forms. Non-technical colleagues get access to data without learning SQL.

It generates REST and GraphQL APIs for tables, supports permissions and webhooks, and offers automation and an AI assistant to help with fields and queries. Because it is open source, teams can host it themselves and keep data on their own servers.

item.title: Prezi
item.description:
Prezi stands out for its zooming interface. Instead of a linear deck, you lay out ideas spatially on a big canvas and the presentation moves among them with motion, which gives viewers a sense of how topics relate and can make a talk feel more dynamic. The approach suits overview-and-detail stories and keeps attention better for some audiences than traditional slides.

The product line has expanded. Prezi Video overlays presentation content next to the speaker on video calls and recordings, Prezi Design creates interactive visual content, and the AI assistant generates presentations from a prompt, rewrites text, and builds structure. Templates, brand kits, and analytics help teams use it for sales, teaching, and training.

item.title: TattooJinn
item.description:
TattooJinn narrows image generation to tattoo art. A user types an idea and picks a style, such as traditional, fine line, or blackwork, and the tool creates design concepts. Variations help someone test placement and look before committing.

The designs work as inspiration for conversations with a tattoo artist, who adapts them to a body and a technique. AI images may include details that do not translate well to skin or may resemble existing artists’ work, so an artist should redraw or approve anything permanent.

item.title: Esko
item.description:
Esko serves the packaging and label industries. Designers use ArtiosCAD to create the structural design of boxes and cartons, with dielines that show cuts and folds. ArtPro+ and related tools prepare artwork for printing, handling color, trapping, and layout across the many steps between a design and the press.

Workflow tools automate preparation and approval. Software checks files for errors, compares versions, and routes proofs, which reduces mistakes in printed packaging where a typo can mean a costly reprint. Cloud platforms support collaboration between brands, designers, and printers, and AI helps with checking and automating routine tasks.

item.title: Perfect365
item.description:
Perfect365 started as a makeover app. A user takes or uploads a selfie, and face detection places virtual makeup, such as lipstick, eyeshadow, and foundation, or changes hair color. Retouching tools smooth skin and adjust features.

Salons and beauty professionals use virtual try-on to help clients picture a result, which supports decisions and sales. It is also popular for social media photos.

Heavy retouching can distort self-image, so use with care, and check the privacy policy since the app processes face photos. It is free with ads and paid options. Alternatives include YouCam Makeup, Facetune, FaceApp, and Modiface. Perfect365 suits casual users and beauty professionals.

item.title: Claude Slides
item.description:
Claude Slides makes decks from a conversation. You describe the audience and the point of the presentation, share notes or source files, and Claude produces a set of slides with an outline, text, and layout. You can then ask for changes, such as a different order, a tighter message, or new visuals, and edit individual slides directly.

The finished deck can be presented from within Claude or exported to PowerPoint or PDF for use elsewhere. Because it lives in the same place as the conversation, you can pull information from uploaded documents and revise based on feedback without switching tools. It sits alongside Claude’s other creation features, including Docs.

item.title: MagicShot
item.description:
MagicShot takes an all-in-one approach to generative media. Rather than paying for a different service for each task, users get a single workspace for generating images, creating video, building avatars, making product shots, and producing voiceovers, all drawing on one pool of credits.

That suits marketers and small businesses who need a bit of everything. Tools include background replacement, upscaling, style transfer, and templates for ads and social posts. Convenience comes with some compromise, as individual tools may be less advanced than specialized products.

item.title: Free AI Face Swap
item.description:
Free AI Face Swap lets a user upload two photos and exchange the faces. The tool detects faces, aligns them, and blends the result. It runs in the browser, supports common image formats, and offers extra effects around face editing.

People use face swaps for entertainment, memes, and creative projects. The same technology can be misused to create misleading or non-consensual images, so use only photos of people who have agreed, and never use swaps to deceive or harass. Many places have laws about deepfakes and intimate image abuse.

item.title: FLUX
item.description: FLUX comes from Black Forest Labs, a company founded by researchers who previously worked on Stable Diffusion. Its models became popular because they produce sharp, detailed images that follow prompts closely, including difficult cases like readable text in a picture and complex scenes with several subjects. For many people, FLUX became the best open alternative to closed services such as Midjourney, because the weights for several versions can be downloaded and used locally.

item.title: GPT Image
item.description:
GPT Image brings image generation into the same model family that handles text. A user describes an image or uploads one to edit, and the model generates or modifies it, following detailed instructions and rendering readable text, which earlier image models struggled with. It can edit photos, change styles, and keep a subject consistent across images.

The model is available inside ChatGPT, where conversation lets users refine results step by step, and through the API for developers building apps. It replaced the DALL-E models in OpenAI’s lineup. Smaller and faster variants exist for cost-sensitive use.

item.title: Stable Diffusion
item.description:
Stable Diffusion changed image generation by being openly available. Rather than a service you rent, the models can be downloaded and run on a consumer GPU, which let anyone generate images privately and without per-image fees. Starting from prompts, the models create pictures in many styles, and later versions improved quality, resolution, and text rendering. Stability AI released several generations, including larger models for higher quality.

A huge ecosystem grew around it. Interfaces such as ComfyUI and Automatic1111 give control over the process, ControlNet guides composition from poses or sketches, and LoRAs let people fine-tune styles or characters with a small number of images. Communities share thousands of models, and hosted services like NightCafe, Leonardo, and Mage.space offer it in the browser. Developers embed the models in applications and pipelines.

item.title: Muse Image
item.description:
Muse Image brings Meta’s own image model to its apps. Users describe an image in the Meta AI app, or create pictures in Instagram Stories and WhatsApp, and the model generates it. Meta says the model reasons about a prompt before drawing, rather than mapping text directly to pixels, which helps with complex requests.

Meta plans to extend it to more surfaces, including Facebook, Messenger, and tools for advertisers. Because it is built into apps with billions of users, it makes image creation available to people who would never open a dedicated generator.

item.title: Nano Banana Pro
item.description:
Nano Banana is the name Google gave to its Gemini-based image model, and the Pro version targets higher quality. Users describe an image or edit a photo by instruction, such as changing the background or combining subjects, and the model produces a result that keeps people and objects consistent.

It is known for rendering legible text inside images, producing high-resolution output, and following detailed prompts, which makes it useful for posters, infographics, and product mockups. It is available in the Gemini app, through Google AI Studio and the API, and in other Google products.

item.title: Cutout.Pro
item.description:
Cutout.Pro offers a set of web tools for common image tasks. Its background remover isolates a subject in a few seconds, and other features upscale resolution, colorize old photos, remove objects, retouch portraits, and generate passport-style photos. A bulk processing option helps stores prepare many product photos.

An API lets developers build these functions into their own products, and plugins connect with tools like Photoshop. Creators and sellers use it for listing photos, social content, and design assets, often at lower cost than hiring a retoucher.

item.title: Gencraft
item.description:
Gencraft aims at casual creators. A user types a description, picks a style such as anime, photo, or fantasy, and gets images in seconds. A mobile app makes it easy to generate avatars, wallpapers, and social media content, and photo transformation tools restyle uploaded pictures.

The platform has added video generation, letting users animate images or generate short clips from prompts. A community feed shows what others create and offers prompts to borrow. The app is designed for experimentation more than for professional workflows.

item.title: Let's Enhance
item.description:
Let’s Enhance takes a small or low-quality image and makes it larger. The AI adds plausible detail as it increases resolution, so a photo can be printed bigger or used on a high-resolution display with less blur. It also reduces noise and compression artifacts and improves color and lighting.

E-commerce sellers use it to improve product photos, designers to rescue old assets, and photographers to prepare prints. Batch processing and an API handle large volumes, and extra tools cover background removal and image generation.

item.title: Magic Patterns
item.description:
Magic Patterns turns an idea into a working interface. A user describes a screen or component, or uploads a screenshot or design, and the tool generates a React prototype that can be previewed and edited through chat or directly. It can follow a team’s design system so the result looks like the real product.

Designers and product managers use it to explore ideas and share clickable prototypes, and developers use it to get a head start on code. Features include collaboration, version history, and export to code or to Figma.

item.title: Magnific AI
item.description:
Magnific is known as a creative upscaler. Where a standard upscaler sharpens existing pixels, Magnific uses generative AI to invent plausible detail, such as skin texture, fabric, foliage, and architectural elements, guided by a prompt and sliders for how much the image should change. The results can be striking, especially for AI-generated art.

The tool also supports style transfer, relighting, and other transformations, and its capabilities have been added to Freepik’s broader creative platform. Freepik acquired Magnific and kept it as a distinct brand, offering API access to its upscaling features.

item.title: Palette.fm
item.description:
Palette.fm adds color to old photos. A user uploads a black-and-white image, and the AI predicts plausible colors for skin, clothing, sky, and objects, returning a colorized version in seconds. Different style options change the overall palette, and results can be refined.

Families use it for old portraits, and historians and archivists use it to make collections more engaging. Colorization is an educated guess based on learned patterns, so colors may not match the real scene, and it should not be presented as historically accurate.

item.title: Prome AI
item.description:
Prome AI helps designers see concepts early. A user uploads a sketch, a screenshot of a 3D model, or a reference photo and writes a prompt, and the tool produces a realistic rendering with chosen materials, lighting, and style. This speeds up exploration before detailed modeling.

Architects use it for building massing and facades, interior designers for room concepts, and product designers for form studies. Variations can be generated quickly to compare options with clients.

item.title: Stockcake
item.description:
Stockcake offers a searchable library of images made with AI. Users browse or search by topic, preview photos, and download them for use in websites, presentations, and social posts without payment or attribution in many cases. The library is aimed at covering common stock needs.

The advantage is speed and no cost. The drawbacks are those of AI imagery: oddities in hands or text, a generic look, and uncertain legal protection around AI-generated content and likenesses. People depicted are not real, which avoids model release issues.

item.title: Vizcom
item.description:
Vizcom speeds up concept design. A designer draws a rough sketch of a shoe, car, or gadget, picks materials or style, and Vizcom generates a realistic render, which can be refined with further drawing and prompts. It can also turn renders into 3D models.

Teams use it to explore many ideas quickly and communicate them to stakeholders. Collaboration tools allow shared workspaces and feedback. Automotive, footwear, and consumer product designers are common users.

item.title: Datawrapper
item.description:
Datawrapper was built by journalists for journalists. A user pastes or uploads data, chooses a chart type such as a bar, line, scatter plot, or map, and adjusts labels, colors, and annotations. The result is a responsive graphic that works on phones and desktops, and can be embedded in a story or exported as an image.

Its design defaults follow good data visualization practice, so charts look clear without fiddling. Features include color-blind friendly palettes, tables with inline bars, locator maps, and a way to update charts automatically from a linked data source. News organizations around the world use it, and teams can share themes to keep a consistent style.

item.title: Perfect Corp
item.description:
Perfect Corp makes AI and augmented reality tools for beauty and fashion. Its skin analysis reads a selfie, scores concerns, and recommends products, while virtual try-on shows makeup, hair color, and accessories on the user’s face in real time.

Brands embed the technology in their websites, apps, and in-store screens to help shoppers choose and reduce returns. Clinics use simulations to show likely effects of treatments. The company also owns the YouCam consumer apps.

item.title: Adobe Firefly
item.description: Firefly is Adobe’s generative AI platform. The Firefly web app generates images from a text description, extends or edits existing ones, creates short video clips, and produces audio and vector artwork. Adobe trained its own models on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it markets them as safer for commercial use than models trained on scraped images. Outputs carry content credentials that note they were made with AI.

item.title: Adobe Lightroom AI
item.description:
Lightroom is built for photographers who handle many images. It organizes a library, lets you rate and filter, and edits photos non-destructively with sliders for exposure, color, tone, and detail. Edits can be copied across a whole shoot, which saves hours after a wedding or event. Lightroom syncs between desktop, phone, and the web, while Lightroom Classic is the desktop-only version with a more traditional file-based workflow.

AI has changed the way people edit in it. Masking tools select the subject, sky, background, or people with a click, so you can adjust one part of a photo without painting a selection. Denoise cleans up high-ISO images while preserving detail, Generative Remove deletes distractions, and Lens Blur adds realistic background blur. Adaptive presets adjust to the content of each photo, and auto-edit settings give a starting point.

item.title: Adobe Sensei
item.description: Sensei is not an app you open. It is the label Adobe uses for the AI and machine learning that runs inside its products, from Photoshop and Premiere Pro to Lightroom, Acrobat, and the Experience Cloud marketing tools. When Photoshop selects a subject in one click, Premiere reframes a video for vertical, or Lightroom masks a sky automatically, that is Sensei doing the work. Many of these features arrived before generative AI became popular, and they handle analysis and automation more than image creation.

item.title: Airtable
item.description: Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a database. Records live in tables with typed fields such as dates, attachments, checkboxes, and links to records in other tables, which allows relationships that spreadsheets cannot handle. The same data can be shown as a grid, kanban board, calendar, gallery, or timeline, and filters and groups tailor each view. It’s used for content calendars, product roadmaps, CRM, event planning, and operations.

item.title: Artbreeder
item.description: Artbreeder began with an unusual idea: instead of typing a prompt, you start with existing images and breed them together, like mixing genes. Each image has sliders for traits, such as age, expression, or lighting for a portrait, so you can nudge it in a direction and save the results. Children of images can be crossed again, which lets a visual idea evolve step by step. The community shares images that others can remix.

item.title: Beautiful.ai
item.description:
Beautiful.ai tackles a common complaint about PowerPoint: you spend more time fiddling with alignment than thinking about content. Its slides are built from smart templates that rearrange themselves when you add or remove text, images, or chart elements, so the design stays clean. Rules keep spacing, fonts, and colors consistent, and a library of layouts covers timelines, comparisons, charts, team slides, and more.

AI features help create the first draft. You can describe a presentation, or paste in notes, and it generates an outline and slides in the app’s format, which you then edit. Teams can store brand colors, fonts, and logos in a shared theme, share slide libraries, and collaborate on decks with comments. Presentations can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF, or shared by link with view analytics.

item.title: BeFunky
item.description:
BeFunky is a browser-based editor for people who want quick results without learning Photoshop. The photo editor has sliders for exposure and color, crop and resize tools, and a large set of filters and effects. A collage maker arranges photos into layouts, and the graphic designer tool offers templates for social media posts, flyers, and cards. Everything runs in a web page, with mobile access too.

AI tools handle common edits. An enhancer sharpens and improves photos, a background remover cuts out subjects, and retouching tools smooth skin and remove blemishes. Artistic effects turn photos into paintings or cartoons, and an upscaler increases resolution. Newer features add AI image generation and a way to remove objects. Many of these are one-click operations, which is the main appeal.

item.title: Bubble
item.description:
Bubble lets people build real web apps without programming. The editor works by placing elements on a page, defining a database, and setting up workflows that say what happens when a user clicks or a condition occurs. Apps can include logins, payments, and integrations with other services.

It is used for marketplaces, internal tools, SaaS products, and prototypes, and some companies run substantial businesses on it. AI features can generate a starting app or page layout from a description, and plugins extend functionality. Bubble hosts the app, so there is no server to manage.

item.title: Canva
item.description: For infographics, Canva works as a template-first editor. You choose a layout for a process, timeline, comparison, statistic, or report, then replace the placeholder text and swap in your own colors and fonts. The element library supplies icons, illustrations, shapes, and photos, and chart tools let you paste or upload numbers to draw bar charts, pie charts, and other graphs that update when the data changes. Because it is a drag-and-drop tool, people without design training can produce something tidy in under an hour.

item.title: Canva
item.description: Canva is a design tool for people who are not designers. You start from a template, swap in your own text and photos, and export the result, which cuts out most of the layout decisions that make design software hard to learn. It covers social media posts, presentations, flyers, resumes, posters, short videos, whiteboards, and simple websites in one editor. A built-in library of photos, graphics, fonts, and music means most projects can be finished without leaving the app.

item.title: Civitai
item.description:
Civitai is where much of the open-source image generation community meets. Creators upload checkpoints, LoRAs, embeddings, and other add-ons for Stable Diffusion, FLUX, and related models, together with sample images and the prompts used. Others download them to run locally in tools like ComfyUI or Automatic1111, or try them in the browser. Ratings, comments, and example galleries make it easier to judge a model before downloading.

The site offers more than a library. Users can generate images on Civitai’s servers using credits, train their own LoRAs from a set of images, and take part in challenges and bounties that reward creators. Articles and guides share techniques, and a point system pays for the use of the site’s services. It became the unofficial catalog for community-trained styles, characters, and concepts.

item.title: Cleanup.pictures
item.description:
Cleanup.pictures does one thing with minimal effort. Upload a photo, brush over a stranger in the background, a power line, a logo, or a blemish, and the tool removes it and fills the gap with a plausible background. Results come back within seconds and can be downloaded, which makes it a quick fix for product photos, real estate listings, travel pictures, and social media posts.

It works well on simple backgrounds such as sky, grass, walls, and water, and less well when the removed object sits in front of detailed patterns, faces, or text that the model would have to invent. For larger images, a higher-resolution output is available on paid plans. The same kind of inpainting appears in other tools, including Clipdrop, which offers a related cleanup feature, along with Photoshop’s Generative Fill and Remove tool and the Magic Eraser on Google Pixel phones.

item.title: ComfyUI
item.description: ComfyUI gives you precise control over generative AI by showing the whole pipeline. Instead of a prompt box and a button, you assemble a graph: load a model, encode a prompt, set up a sampler, add LoRAs or ControlNet for guidance, upscale, and save. Each step is a node you can inspect and rewire. It started with Stable Diffusion and now supports many image, video, and audio models, including FLUX, so new models are often usable in ComfyUI first.

item.title: Craiyon
item.description:
Craiyon began as DALL-E mini, an open-source experiment that went viral for producing odd, low-resolution images from text prompts. It was one of the first image generators many people tried, and it popularized the idea that anyone could make pictures with words. The site then rebranded as Craiyon and kept its low barrier to entry: open the page, type a prompt, and wait for the results.

The quality has improved with newer models, and Craiyon now produces more detailed images in several styles, including photos, illustrations, and drawings. Paid plans remove ads, speed up generation, and add features such as faster queues, higher resolution, and a private mode. The tool is positioned for casual use, like quick illustrations, memes, and idea sketches, instead of professional production.

item.title: Decktopus
item.description: Decktopus is built for people who need a presentation quickly. You enter a topic or a short brief, answer a few questions about the audience and goal, and the AI produces an outline and a deck of designed slides with suggested images and speaker notes. You then edit the text and layout in a drag-and-drop editor. It also offers templates for pitches, reports, and sales decks, and a brand kit for colors and logos.

item.title: Dream by WOMBO
item.description: Dream by WOMBO is aimed at casual creators who want to see their ideas as art without learning prompt techniques. You type a phrase, pick a style such as oil painting, anime, fantasy, or neon, and the app returns an image in a few seconds. The style menu does much of the work that detailed prompts would do in other tools, which makes it approachable on a phone. It is popular for profile pictures, wallpapers, and quick social posts.

item.title: Figma
item.description: Figma is where a lot of software gets designed before anyone writes code. It runs in the browser, so designers, product managers, engineers, and writers can open the same file at once, leave comments, and watch changes appear live. That ended the old habit of emailing design files back and forth. Its core strengths are vector editing, Auto Layout for components that resize correctly, and shared libraries that keep colors, type, and buttons consistent across a whole product.

item.title: Freepik AI
item.description: Freepik began as a stock site for vectors, photos, and icons, and many designers already knew it. It has added a full AI suite on top. The image generator creates pictures from text prompts, and tools for editing, upscaling, retouching, and expanding images let users refine them. Video generation and animation features turn stills or prompts into short clips, and a workspace organizes projects and lets you mix different tools.

item.title: Gamma
item.description:
Gamma reimagined the presentation. Instead of slides built from a blank template, you describe what you want, such as a pitch for a new product or a lesson on photosynthesis, and Gamma generates a complete, designed deck with text, layouts, and images. The format uses flexible cards that expand and collapse, so presentations can feel more like interactive documents, and it also produces documents and one-page websites.

Editing is conversational and visual. You can ask the AI to rewrite a section, change the style, add images, or restructure, or edit manually with simple controls. Themes keep designs consistent, brand settings apply company fonts and colors, and sharing by link includes analytics on who viewed it. Decks can be exported to PowerPoint or PDF, and it integrates with other tools.

item.title: Generated Photos
item.description:
Generated Photos solves a licensing problem: real people’s faces carry privacy and consent obligations, and stock photos can be expensive or restrictive. Its library holds images of faces created by generative models, which depict nobody in particular. Designers use them for website and app mockups, marketers for illustrations, and developers for placeholder avatars in user interfaces.

Several tools extend the library. A face generator lets you pick attributes such as age, gender, ethnicity, hair, and emotion and create new faces, and a photo anonymizer replaces a real face in a picture with a synthetic one. Datasets of synthetic faces serve machine learning teams who need varied images without privacy concerns, and an API provides access for automated use. Full-body and other synthetic image options have been added.

item.title: GetIMG.ai
item.description: getimg.ai provides a web workspace for creating and editing images with AI. You can generate pictures from a prompt using a choice of models, including Stable Diffusion variants and other leading generators, then refine them. Tools for inpainting let you replace part of an image, outpainting extends it past its borders, and an infinite canvas allows you to compose scenes from several generations. Upscaling, background removal, and face tools help finish the result.

item.title: Infogram
item.description:
Infogram helps turn numbers into visual stories. You choose a template for an infographic, report, chart, or dashboard, import data from a spreadsheet or connect to a live source, and customize the design with your brand colors and fonts. The tool produces polished charts and maps, many of them interactive, that can be embedded on websites or shared as links.

Several features support data communication. Over thirty chart types, including maps and tables, handle different kinds of data, and live data connections update visuals when the source changes. Teams can collaborate on projects, keep brand templates, and publish with analytics. Downloads include images and PDFs, and AI features help generate visuals and suggest ways to present data.

item.title: InVision
item.description:
InVision was one of the leading prototyping and design collaboration tools of the 2010s. Designers uploaded static screens, linked them into clickable prototypes, and shared them with stakeholders for feedback. It also offered a design system manager and, later, Freehand, a collaborative whiteboard.

As Figma and other tools took over design work, InVision’s usage declined, and the company announced it would close its products. Teams moved their work to other platforms, and exports were offered for a period before shutdown.

item.title: Lensa AI
item.description:
Lensa is a mobile photo editor best known for a single viral feature. Magic Avatars let users upload a set of selfies and receive a collection of stylized portraits in the style of fantasy art, anime, or illustration. The effect spread quickly on social media, driving downloads and making many people aware of AI image generation. The avatars are created with a model fine-tuned on each user’s photos.

The core of the app is a selfie and portrait editor. It offers retouching for skin and eyes, background replacement, blur and sharpening, and a range of filters and effects. Subscribers get access to the full tool set, and Magic Avatars can be purchased as packs. Prisma Labs, the developer, also makes other photo and AI apps.

item.title: Lucidchart AI
item.description:
Lucidchart is a mature online diagramming tool from Lucid Software. Users create flowcharts, process maps, org charts, wireframes, network diagrams, and technical drawings with a large library of shapes and templates, and collaborate in real time with comments and version history. Because it runs in the browser and integrates with the tools that teams already use, it’s popular in business and IT.

Several features go beyond drawing. Data linking can generate org charts or network diagrams from spreadsheets and cloud accounts, so diagrams stay current, and a presentation mode turns diagrams into slides. AI features generate diagrams from a text description, suggest improvements, and summarize complex drawings. Lucidchart is part of the Lucid suite, which also includes Lucidspark for whiteboarding and Lucidscale for cloud diagrams.

item.title: Mage.space
item.description:
Mage.space gives people a simple front end for open-source image models. You choose from a catalog of checkpoints, write a prompt, adjust settings like style, size, and number of images, and generate. It supports image-to-image transformations, inpainting, and control features that guide composition, and results can be upscaled. Because it hosts the models, users do not need a powerful computer or a local installation.

The platform appeals to people who want flexibility in styles, from realistic photos to anime and fantasy art, and who want to experiment with community-trained models. It has a gallery of public creations, and a text-to-video tool has been added to some plans. Content rules are looser than on some mainstream services, though it still prohibits illegal material.

item.title: Microsoft Designer
item.description:
Microsoft Designer helps people make graphics quickly. You describe what you want, such as an invitation for a birthday party or a banner for a sale, and Designer produces several layout options with text, images, and styling, which you can edit. It offers templates for common formats, background removal, and tools for resizing a design for different platforms.

AI image generation is built in, powered by Microsoft’s and OpenAI’s image models, so you can create custom illustrations or photos to include in a design. It integrates with Microsoft 365 apps and Copilot, and is available on the web, as a mobile app, and inside tools such as Edge. Brand kits and shared templates are available on paid Microsoft 365 plans.

item.title: Midjourney
item.description: Midjourney is one of the most popular image generators, valued for its distinctive aesthetic. You describe an image, and it returns variations that tend to look polished and painterly, with strong composition and lighting. It began on Discord, where users type commands in a shared channel, and now offers a web interface with an image editor, personal galleries, and organization tools. It’s widely used by illustrators, designers, concept artists, and marketers.

item.title: Neural.love
item.description:
Neural.love combines creation and repair tools in one web app. The generator creates images from text prompts with a choice of models and styles, while the enhancement tools improve existing pictures. Upscaling increases resolution, denoising cleans grainy photos, and restoration repairs scratches and faded color on old family pictures. Face enhancement can sharpen portraits, and colorization adds color to black-and-white images.

The platform is practical for photographers, genealogists, designers, and anyone with old or low-quality images. Users upload a file, choose the effect, and download the result, with credits consumed by each operation. An API lets developers add enhancement features to their own apps, and batch options handle many images. Generated images can be used in marketing and design, subject to the terms for each plan.

item.title: ON1 Photo AI
item.description:
ON1 Photo AI aims to shorten the path from a raw photo to a finished image. It analyzes a picture and suggests adjustments, then applies tools such as NoNoise AI for removing grain, Sharpener AI for restoring detail, and Super Resolution for enlarging photos. Other tools handle sky replacement, background removal, portrait retouching, and object removal, and automatic masking selects subjects, skies, and other regions for local edits.

It fits into several workflows. It can open and process RAW files directly, work as a standalone app, or run as a plugin inside Lightroom, Photoshop, and other editors, which lets photographers use its AI tools without leaving their usual software. Presets provide quick looks, and batch processing handles many images at once. A separate ON1 Photo RAW product adds organizing and layer-based editing.

item.title: Penpot
item.description:
Penpot is built for collaboration between designers and developers. It uses open web standards, so designs map to real code, and supports flexible layouts based on CSS grid and flex. Teams create prototypes, design systems, and shared components in a browser.

Being open source matters to some teams. They can host Penpot themselves, keep control of their data, and avoid vendor lock-in, and developers can inspect designs and get code in a familiar form. AI features and plugins extend the tool.

item.title: Picsart AI
item.description:
Picsart began as a mobile photo editor and grew into a broad creative suite. Users edit photos with filters, collages, stickers, and text, make videos, and design social posts from templates. A community lets people share and remix content, which helped it spread among younger creators and small businesses.

AI is now central. Tools generate images from prompts, remove backgrounds and objects, expand pictures, replace elements, enhance and upscale photos, and create stylized avatars. Text-to-video and animation tools turn ideas into clips, and an AI writer helps with captions. Picsart also provides APIs and plugins so other platforms can use its image tools, and teams can use brand kits and shared workspaces.

item.title: Piktochart
item.description: Piktochart is aimed at people who need to present information visually but are not designers. You choose a template for an infographic, report, presentation, or poster, edit the text and images, and add charts and maps that you can link to data. Visual blocks, icons, illustrations, and a library of graphics make it quick to produce clean results, and the tool exports to image and PDF formats or shares online.

item.title: Pitch
item.description:
Pitch aims to make presentations that look good without wrestling with layouts. It provides modern templates, smart slide types, and a brand-aware design system that keeps a team’s decks consistent. Collaboration works like a shared document: several people edit at once, leave comments, and track versions, which suits startups, agencies, and sales teams that produce decks together.

Distinctive features include presentation analytics and sharing. You can send a deck as a link and see who viewed it and for how long, which is helpful for investor and sales decks, and recordings let you narrate a deck for asynchronous sharing. AI tools generate slide drafts from a prompt, rewrite text, and create visuals, and the platform integrates with tools like Slack, HubSpot, and Google Drive.

item.title: Pixelcut
item.description:
Pixelcut focuses on product images. A seller photographs an item, removes the background in one tap, and places the product on a clean or styled backdrop. AI can generate scenes that suit a product, add shadows, and upscale low-resolution pictures.

Batch tools process many images, and templates help create ads, social posts, and listing graphics. The mobile app is popular with small sellers who shoot products with a phone.

Pixelcut has a free tier and paid plans. AI-generated scenes should still show the product accurately to avoid returns. Alternatives include Photoroom, Canva, Pebblely, Remove.bg, and Adobe Express. Pixelcut suits small online sellers.

item.title: Plasmic
item.description:
Plasmic connects visual design with real code. Developers register their React components in Plasmic, and designers and marketers can then drag those components onto a canvas, adjust styling and content, and publish pages without waiting for a code release. Alternatively, Plasmic can build entire pages and sites itself, and its output integrates with frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, and plain React.

Features help teams collaborate. A CMS stores content, responsive design controls handle layouts across devices, and the editor includes interactions, animations, and data bindings. Teams can use it to build landing pages, marketing sites, and web apps, while developers stay in control of the underlying components. Code can be exported or used with a runtime, which reduces lock-in.

item.title: Playground AI
item.description:
Playground started as a place to experiment with image models in a friendly interface. You enter a prompt, choose a model and style, and generate images, then refine them in a canvas that lets you edit parts of a picture, combine elements, and iterate. It was positioned as a flexible tool for artists, designers, and marketers, with a free daily allowance that made it popular for experimentation.

The company has also developed its own image models, which it has promoted for following prompts closely and rendering text, along with tools for creating logos, posters, and social graphics. Image-to-image, upscaling, and editing by instruction help refine results. Users can browse a community feed to see what others are making and borrow ideas.

item.title: Plus AI
item.description:
Plus AI takes the approach that you shouldn’t have to leave your slide editor to use AI. After installing the add-in in Google Slides or PowerPoint, you describe the presentation you want, and it drafts an outline and slides in the editor, which you can then adjust like any other deck. It can also build from a document, a set of notes, or a web page.

Editing features save time on existing decks. The remix tool can restyle or rework slides, and the rewrite function changes tone or length of text on a slide. It can convert content into a different layout, summarize, and create speaker notes. Because the output is native slides, the file remains fully editable and compatible with company templates and brand assets.

item.title: Remini
item.description:
Remini gained a following for photo restoration. A user uploads an old family photo or a blurry picture, and the AI sharpens it, repairs damage, and enhances faces. It can also upscale images and colorize black-and-white ones.

The app expanded into AI-generated portraits and avatars from selfies, which went viral at times. Video enhancement is also offered. It runs mainly on phones, with processing in the cloud.

Remini has a free tier with ads and limits, and paid plans, and has faced criticism over subscription practices. Enhancement invents plausible detail, so faces may change from the original. Photos are uploaded, so check the privacy policy. Alternatives include Topaz Photo AI, Let’s Enhance, Photoshop’s neural filters, VanceAI, and Palette.fm. Remini suits people restoring family photos.

item.title: SeaArt
item.description: SeaArt gives users a rich set of image generation tools in a friendly interface. You write a prompt, choose among many models and styles, and generate images, with options such as ControlNet to guide pose or composition and LoRA models to apply particular styles or characters. A library of community-shared models, workflows, and characters lets users build on others’ work, and a node-based workflow editor offers more advanced control for those who want it.

item.title: Sketch
item.description:
Sketch helped define modern interface design. Designers create screens with vectors and reusable symbols, build design systems, and prototype interactions. Its Mac-native app is fast and has a large plugin ecosystem.

Collaboration moved to the web, where teammates view, comment, and hand off designs, and a Windows-compatible web editor extends access. AI features help generate placeholder content, adjust layouts, and speed up repetitive work.

Sketch is sold by subscription. Figma has taken much of its market because of browser-based collaboration. Alternatives include Figma, Penpot, Adobe XD (no longer developed), Framer, and Affinity Designer. Sketch suits Mac-based designers who prefer a native tool.

item.title: Slidebean
item.description:
Slidebean separates writing from design. You enter text for each slide in an outline-style editor, choose a slide type such as problem, solution, market, or team, and the software lays it out, selecting fonts, spacing, and graphics so the result looks professional. That means founders can focus on the message and avoid spending hours on layout. AI features help draft slide content and improve wording.

Because it was built for startups, Slidebean adds extras beyond slides. It offers pitch deck templates based on successful funding decks, tools to share decks and see who viewed them, and a financial model builder for projections. The company has also offered pitch deck design and fundraising services for founders who want expert help.

item.title: SlidesAI
item.description:
SlidesAI works inside Google Slides. You paste in text, such as an essay, notes, or an article, or enter a topic, and the add-on creates a set of slides with titles, bullet points, and layout. It lets you pick a presentation style, color theme, and the number of slides, and can add relevant images. The result is a draft that you edit like any other Google Slides deck.

Additional features support content work. It can summarize long text into key points, paraphrase for clarity, and generate text for slides from a prompt. Because the output is a native Slides file, it can be shared, collaborated on, and presented as usual. It’s popular with students, teachers, and professionals who need a quick starting point.

item.title: StarryAI
item.description:
StarryAI brought AI art generation to phones. In the app, you enter a text prompt, pick an art style or model, and receive images within a minute or so. Styles range from fantasy and anime to realism and abstract, and you can use an image as a starting point for variations. It’s aimed at hobbyists and creators who want art for wallpapers, profile pictures, book covers, or game concepts.

Features support experimentation. You can control aspect ratio, choose among models, and upscale results, and a gallery shows creations from other users for inspiration. Different pricing tiers offer more credits and faster generation, and the terms for commercial use vary by plan, with ownership of outputs depending on the subscription.

item.title: StockImg AI
item.description:
StockImg AI turns a description into a usable image. Instead of searching a stock library for something close to what you imagine, you type what you want and the tool creates it. It offers separate generators geared to common needs: logo designs, ebook and book covers, posters, wallpapers, illustrations, and app screen mockups. Each has settings suited to its format, such as aspect ratios for covers and posters.

The tool also includes editing functions. You can adjust and regenerate images, remove backgrounds, and explore variations. Self-publishers, small businesses, bloggers, and social media managers use it to get covers and graphics without hiring a designer or paying for licenses. The output is meant to be unique to your prompt, which avoids the problem of the same stock photo showing up in many places.

item.title: Tome
item.description:
Tome became a popular early example of generative AI for presentations. A user described a topic, and Tome produced a complete, designed narrative with text, images, and layout, which could be edited in a flexible, canvas-like format. It was positioned as a more modern, storytelling-focused alternative to PowerPoint, and gained millions of users, with attention from students, founders, and professionals.

The company later decided to retire the presentation product and pivot to something different, a sales-focused application. Users were given a period to export their work before the service closed. The pivot reflected a challenge facing many AI tools: general features are quickly matched by larger products, and a standalone app needs a defensible niche.

item.title: Topaz Photo AI
item.description:
Topaz Photo AI aims to fix the technical flaws in photos with little effort. When you open an image, it analyzes the content and suggests corrections, using models for noise reduction, sharpening, and increasing resolution. It handles problems like grainy high-ISO shots, soft focus, and motion blur, and can enlarge photos while adding believable detail. Many wildlife, sports, and event photographers use it to rescue difficult images.

The tool also offers face recovery, light adjustment, color balance, and a way to apply different adjustments to selected subjects. It can be run as a standalone application, as an external editor from Lightroom, or as a plugin for Photoshop, and processes batches of images. Models run locally on your computer and benefit from a good graphics card.

item.title: Upscayl
item.description: Upscayl makes AI upscaling available to anyone. You drag in a low-resolution image, choose a model, and the app enlarges it by two, three, or four times with added detail, saving the result to your computer. It includes models tuned for general photos, digital art, and sharpening, and supports batch processing for many files. Because it runs on your own hardware, there is no per-image fee, and your images stay private.

item.title: Vectorizer.ai
item.description:
Vectorizer.ai converts bitmap images into vectors, which are scalable files used for logos, print, and cutting machines. Upload a low-resolution logo or illustration, and the service traces the shapes into paths and fills, returning an SVG, EPS, PDF, or DXF that can be resized without losing sharpness. The AI approach produces cleaner curves and fewer stray points than older tracing tools, with controls to adjust the level of detail.

Designers use it to recover logos from low-quality files, sign makers and crafters use it to prepare artwork for vinyl cutters and laser engravers, and developers add it to workflows through an API. It handles flat-color artwork best, such as logos and icons, and it works less well on photographs, which turn into complex tracings with many shapes. A preview lets you see the result before paying.

item.title: Venngage
item.description:
Venngage targets people who need to communicate information visually. Users start from thousands of templates for infographics, reports, flyers, presentations, and social graphics, replace the content, and customize colors, icons, and charts. Data can be imported to generate charts, and the tool includes maps and diagrams for explaining processes and comparisons.

It differentiates itself with business features. Brand kits apply logos, fonts, and colors automatically, team workspaces allow collaboration and approvals, and an accessibility checker flags color contrast and other issues. AI tools generate infographic designs from text, write copy, and suggest improvements, and designs can be exported or shared with analytics.

item.title: Visily
item.description:
Visily is built for people who need to mock up interfaces quickly without learning a full design tool. You can upload a screenshot of an app, a hand-drawn sketch, or a description of a screen, and the AI creates an editable wireframe made of real components. A library of templates, UI kits, and smart components helps assemble screens for web and mobile products.

Collaboration is part of the appeal. Teams can edit together, leave comments, and share clickable prototypes with stakeholders, and designs can be exported or moved into Figma for refinement. Product managers, business analysts, and founders use it to communicate ideas visually and gather feedback early, before engineering work starts.

item.title: Visme AI
item.description:
Visme is aimed at people who need to present information visually without design skills. It offers a drag-and-drop editor with thousands of templates for presentations, infographics, reports, charts, social media posts, and documents. Data widgets create charts and graphs from spreadsheets, and interactive elements such as links and animations can be added. Brand kits keep colors, fonts, and logos consistent across a team.

AI features speed up creation. An AI designer can generate a presentation or document from a prompt, write and rewrite text, create images, and suggest layouts. Teams can collaborate in real time with comments and workflows, and content can be exported as PDF, PowerPoint, or HTML, or shared by link with analytics. Visme is often used by marketers, educators, consultants, and communications teams.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: Whimsical AI
item.description:
Whimsical puts several lightweight visual tools in one place. You can draw flowcharts and sequence diagrams, sketch low-fidelity wireframes, brainstorm on mind maps, write docs, and arrange sticky notes on a board. The tools are designed around speed, with keyboard shortcuts, snapping, and a clean look that makes rough thinking easy to share.

AI features reduce the setup. Describe a process and Whimsical can draft a flowchart, turn a topic into a mind map, or produce a first-pass wireframe, which you then edit by hand. Teams use it for planning, product specs, and explaining systems, and sharing is simple with links, comments, and embeds in tools like Notion and Confluence.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier lets people automate work between apps without programming. A Zap starts with a trigger, such as a new form entry, and performs actions in other apps, like adding a row to a spreadsheet and sending a Slack message. It connects thousands of products.

AI has become part of the platform. Users describe an automation in plain language, add AI steps that summarize or classify data, and build agents that act across apps. Tables, forms, and interfaces let teams build small apps around their automations.

item.title: Lexica
item.description:
Lexica began as a searchable archive of AI-generated images with the prompts that created them. Browsing the archive helped people learn how wording affects results, and copy ideas for their own generations. That made it a popular learning resource in the early days of image generators.

The platform added its own image generation models and an editor, so users can create images, refine them, and organize collections. It offers different model options and tools for art, product shots, and concepts. The community library remains a source of inspiration.

item.title: Lummi
item.description:
Lummi collects AI-generated pictures in a searchable library, organized by category and style. Users browse or search for backgrounds, textures, scenes, and illustrations, then download them for use in websites, presentations, and campaigns. The pitch is variety and a modern look compared with familiar stock photography.

The platform includes generation tools that let users create images from prompts and adjust them, along with options for editing. It is popular with designers who want unusual or abstract visuals and do not want to prompt from scratch.

item.title: Magnific AI
item.description:
Magnific AI takes a low-resolution image and produces a larger version with added, invented detail. Users control how much creative freedom the AI takes with settings such as creativity and resemblance, and can add a prompt describing what the detail should look like. This makes it different from conventional upscalers.

Artists use it to polish AI-generated images and to turn rough concept art into detailed illustrations. Designers use it to prepare images for large formats. The company was acquired by Freepik, and the technology is available through Magnific’s own site and Freepik’s tools.

item.title: PixAI
item.description:
PixAI is built around anime-style generation. Users type prompts, pick models trained for particular looks, and generate images. A feed of community creations offers inspiration, and sharing prompts lets others learn techniques.

Features include image-to-image transformation, model and LoRA libraries, and tools for creating characters consistently. A mobile app and credit system support casual use.

PixAI has a free tier with daily credits and paid plans. Community models can be trained on artwork without artists’ consent, which is controversial, and content rules apply to the platform. Alternatives include Civitai, Leonardo AI, NovelAI, Midjourney with niji, and Tensor.Art. PixAI suits anime fans and illustrators exploring AI art.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Recraft
item.description:
Recraft is aimed at designers. Besides raster images, it can produce true vector graphics, such as logos, icons, and illustrations, that remain sharp at any size and can be edited in design software. Style controls keep outputs consistent across a project.

Brand features let a team upload colors, fonts, and example images so generations follow a style. The model handles text in images well, which helps with posters and mockups. Editing tools allow changing parts of an image, removing backgrounds, and upscaling.

item.title: Stablecog
item.description:
Stablecog offers image generation without the setup of running a model locally. Users enter a prompt, choose a model and settings, and receive images in seconds. The code is open, and the project is run as a community-minded service.

It appeals to hobbyists who want to try Stable Diffusion and its variants and to developers who want a reference for building their own interface. Free credits are available, with paid options for more use.

item.title: Tensor.Art
item.description:
Tensor.Art lets people create images without owning a GPU. They choose from a library of models and LoRAs trained by the community, type a prompt, and generate images, often in styles from anime to realism. Workflows can be remixed, and results shared in a gallery.

The platform supports training custom models, running ComfyUI-based workflows, and generating video, and it has a credit system for heavy use. It appeals to hobbyists and artists who want variety.

item.title: Adobe Express
item.description:
Adobe Express is Adobe’s answer to Canva: a simple editor where you start from a template, change the text and images, and export. It covers social media posts, banners, flyers, simple videos, and quick edits to PDFs. It runs in the browser and on phones, and it needs no design background. Brand kits, shared templates, and a content scheduler help small teams keep their posts consistent.

The AI tools come from Adobe’s Firefly models. You can generate images from a text prompt, extend or fill parts of a photo, apply text effects from a description, remove backgrounds, and resize a design for several platforms in one step. Because it shares libraries with Creative Cloud, assets from Photoshop or Illustrator can be used directly in Express projects, and designers can hand off a template that colleagues then adjust.

item.title: BestPhotoAI
item.description:
BestPhotoAI is meant for fast photo improvement. A user uploads an image, and the tool can sharpen details, increase resolution, fix lighting and color, and retouch skin, then returns an enhanced version. The aim is to save time compared with manual editing in Photoshop or Lightroom.

Typical users are e-commerce sellers who need clean product photos, creators preparing profile and social images, and people restoring older pictures. Automated enhancement works best on ordinary issues like low light or noise, and results vary with the source image.

item.title: Bing Image Creator
item.description: Bing Image Creator made AI image generation easy to try. You type a description, and it returns several images within a few seconds, with no installation and no cost beyond a Microsoft account. Its popularity came from being free and being available inside Bing and Edge, long before many alternatives had a free tier. Microsoft has since renamed the tool Image Creator from Designer and tied it into Copilot and the Designer app.

item.title: ClipDrop
item.description:
Clipdrop packages common image edits into simple web tools. Remove Background cuts out a subject in a click, Cleanup erases unwanted objects, Image Upscaler enlarges small pictures with added detail, and Uncrop extends an image beyond its borders. Relight changes the lighting on a subject, and Replace Background swaps in a new scene from a text prompt. A text-to-image generator rounds out the set, using Stability AI models.

Product photographers, e-commerce sellers, marketers, and casual users reach for it when they need a quick edit without opening a heavy editor. The tools work in the browser and on mobile, with an API for developers who want to add the same features to their own apps. The project had a short stint under Stability AI before moving to Jasper, which acquired it to expand its marketing tools.

item.title: DALL-E 3
item.description:
DALL-E 3 was a text-to-image model known for following detailed prompts closely. Its integration with ChatGPT let users describe an image in conversation and have the assistant refine the prompt, which made image generation accessible to people who had never used a dedicated art tool. Developers could also call it through OpenAI’s API.

It was part of a line that began with the original DALL-E and DALL-E 2, which helped popularize text-to-image generation. Over time, OpenAI moved to newer image models built natively into its multimodal systems, which handle text in images and edits better. DALL-E branding faded as a result.

item.title: Dora
item.description:
Dora targets people who want a standout site without writing code. A user describes the site or starts from a template, and the platform generates pages with 3D objects, scroll animations, and interactions, which are expensive to build by hand. A visual editor lets them adjust layout, copy, and motion.

Designers and small businesses use it for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites where visual impact matters. Compared with simple builders, it emphasizes motion and depth. Published sites are hosted by the platform, and exporting options vary by plan.

item.title: Erase.bg
item.description:
Erase.bg handles one of the most common editing jobs. You upload a picture of a product, person, or object, and an AI model detects the foreground and removes the background, producing a PNG with transparency. It works on people, products, animals, and cars, and handles complex edges like hair reasonably well. Typical users are online sellers, designers, and anyone making a profile picture or a presentation.

Several features make it more practical for volume work. Batch processing lets you upload many images at once, and an API and plugins integrate with design tools and workflows. After removing the background, you can add a solid color, a new image, or leave it transparent. A free tier gives low-resolution results, and paid credits or subscriptions unlock high-resolution downloads.

item.title: Fotor
item.description:
Fotor covers everyday editing for people who do not want Photoshop. In the photo editor, you crop, adjust color and light, apply filters and effects, and retouch portraits by smoothing skin and removing blemishes. A collage maker and a design studio offer templates for social posts, posters, and cards. Everything works in a browser, with matching apps for phones and computers.

AI tools handle the harder steps. One-click enhancement improves exposure and sharpness, background removal makes cutouts, an object remover erases distractions, and an upscaler enlarges small pictures. Newer features include text-to-image generation, avatars, and generative fill for extending or changing parts of an image. Fotor also has an AI video editor for simple clips.

item.title: Galileo AI
item.description:
Galileo AI was one of the early tools for turning a prompt into interface designs. You described a screen, such as a fitness app dashboard or a checkout page, and it produced a detailed, editable design with components, imagery, and layout, which could be copied into Figma and refined. It was popular with product designers and founders as a way to explore ideas and get past the blank canvas.

Google acquired Galileo AI and brought its team and technology into its own design-generation product, Stitch, which creates interfaces from text or images and exports to Figma and code. The standalone Galileo service was wound down as part of that move.

item.title: Ideogram
item.description:
Ideogram became known for solving a problem that frustrated early image generators: spelling. Ask most models for a poster that says “Grand Opening” and you get distorted letters, while Ideogram’s models usually produce clean, legible type in a chosen style. That makes it a practical choice for posters, book covers, t-shirt designs, logos, memes, and social media graphics, where words are part of the image.

It also performs well on general image generation, with strong prompt following across photorealistic, illustrated, and graphic design styles. Beyond generating from scratch, the apps include tools to remove backgrounds, erase objects, resize images for ads, and edit text layers. Teams can use private generation, shared libraries, and custom models, and a developer API provides the same models in other products.

item.title: Khroma
item.description:
Khroma starts by asking you to pick 50 colors you like. A neural network learns your tastes from those choices, then generates an endless stream of color combinations that match your style, shown as palettes, gradients, typography samples, and images. The aim is to make exploring color feel personal instead of random.

Designers use it to find inspiration for brand identities, websites, and illustrations. You can save favorite palettes, view them in different layouts, check color contrast, and search for combinations by a specific color. The interface is minimal and focused on discovery, and everything runs in the browser.

item.title: Krea AI
item.description:
Krea became popular for its real-time canvas. As you type a prompt or sketch shapes, the image updates almost instantly, which turns generation into a live, exploratory process instead of waiting for each result. That immediacy suits designers and artists who iterate visually, adjusting composition and style through gestures rather than rewriting prompts.

The platform has expanded into a wide creative toolkit. It lets you generate images and video with a selection of models from different providers, upscale and enhance images with a strong emphasis on detail, edit existing pictures, and train custom styles from your own examples. Features such as pattern and logo generation, and tools for animating stills, appeal to designers and motion artists. Multiple models in one place make comparison easy.

item.title: Leonardo AI
item.description:
Leonardo.ai began as a tool for game developers who needed lots of consistent assets. Users generate images from text prompts with a choice of Leonardo’s own models and others, then refine them with inpainting, upscaling, and background removal. Fine-tuned models for characters, environments, items, and concept art made it popular with game artists, illustrators, and designers who care about a particular visual style.

Customization is a major draw. You can train your own models on a set of images to produce consistent characters or brand looks, use reference images to control composition and style, and draw on a canvas to guide generation.
